subject: Computer Networking
title: Ethernet: The LAN Standard
description: A 60-second lesson on Ethernet: The LAN Standard.

hook.text: In 1973, Bob Metcalfe sketched a way to connect computers in an office with a shared cable. He called it Ethernet.

buildup.text: Ethernet used a thick coaxial cable. All computers listened on the same wire and took turns transmitting.

discovery.text: CSMA/CD handled collisions: listen before sending, detect conflicts, wait a random time, then retry.

twist.text: Ethernet outlasted every competitor — Token Ring, FDDI, ATM. Simplicity and low cost won the market.

climax.text: Modern Ethernet runs at 400 Gbps over fiber. The protocol evolved but the name and principles endure.

punchline.text: Ethernet won the LAN war through simplicity.

details.summary: Ethernet, invented by Robert Metcalfe at Xerox PARC in 1973, became the dominant technology for local area networks. It used a shared cable where devices took turns transmitting, using a protocol called CSMA/CD to handle collisions. Modern Ethernet uses switches and runs at speeds up to 400 Gbps.
details.whyItMatters: Ethernet won the LAN wars by being simple, cheap, and adaptable. Nearly every wired network connection in the world today uses some form of Ethernet.
takeaways: Ethernet was invented at Xerox PARC in 1973
CSMA/CD managed shared access on early Ethernet networks
Modern Ethernet runs at 400 Gbps using switches, not shared cables

faq.question: How has Ethernet evolved since 1973?
faq.answer: From 2.94 Mbps shared coaxial cable to 400 Gbps switched fiber optic connections. Shared media was replaced by switches that give each device a dedicated connection. The frame format remains recognizable from the original, showing remarkable backward compatibility.

faq.question: Why did Ethernet beat competing LAN technologies?
faq.answer: It was simpler and cheaper than Token Ring and other alternatives. Its design scaled well from small offices to large data centers. Industry standardization through IEEE 802.3 ensured interoperability. Ethernet's adaptability to new speeds and media kept it relevant for decades.
